content.title: About
content.content: Breadsticks NFS are dry, crunchy snack sticks made from wheat flour, water, salt and yeast. They are baked until golden and are often served with sauces, soups, or enjoyed on their own. The flavor is mild and slightly salty, making them versatile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first breadsticks originated in Italy in the 19th century as a way to use leftover dough.
NFS stands for “Low‑Calorie Fermented Snacks,” highlighting their lightness.
They are frequently used in culinary schools to demonstrate dough‑rolling techniques.
Breadsticks can serve as the base for “papa‑apricot” – a snack where a stick is wrapped around cheese and olives.
In some countries they are served with flavored oils, such as rosemary or garlic.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One stick contains about 15–20 kcal, making it suitable for diet‑friendly eating.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Wheat flour provides a slow‑release energy source that helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain versions offer dietary fiber beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Unlike many snack foods, breadsticks contain virtually no fat.

items.title: Provides B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast‑leavened dough retains small amounts of B1, B2 and niacin.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Breadsticks contain wheat flour and are unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some varieties can be heavily salted; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Moisture‑related spoilage
items.content: When stored in humid conditions, sticks can become a breeding ground for mold.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Breadsticks can be eaten plain, dipped in olive oil, sauces, hummus, or cheese spreads. They are often added to soups for crunch or used as a base for canapés, wrapping around cheese, ham or vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, refrigerate to prevent moisture absorption. Follow the expiration date printed on the package.

content.title: About
content.content: Japanese tea cookie is a crisp, dry biscuit flavored with high‑quality green tea (matcha or sencha). It combines a subtle sweetness with the distinctive aroma of Japanese tea, making it an ideal light snack and a perfect accompaniment to tea ceremonies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tea used is often shade‑grown, which boosts the L‑theanine content.
Traditional Japanese biscuits are frequently served alongside matcha in tea houses.
The balance of sweet dough and the slightly bitter tea flavor creates the umami‑sweet harmony typical of Japanese cuisine.
Some versions are dusted with a fine layer of dried matcha powder to intensify the aroma.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Green tea provides catechins that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Contains L‑theanine
items.content: L‑theanine promotes relaxation without drowsiness, enhancing focus.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Compared with many sweets, this cookie typically uses a moderate amount of sugar.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Wheat or rice flour contributes a modest amount of dietary fiber.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Caffeine and catechins in the tea may slightly boost metabolic rate.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The cookie is usually made with wheat flour, which can be problematic for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Green tea caffeine may cause insomnia or jitteriness in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although moderate, people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some commercial versions may contain artificial flavors or preservatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Japanese tea cookies pair wonderfully with a hot cup of matcha, green tea, or even a light milk drink. They can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to dessert platters, or used as a crunchy topping for ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to preserve crunch and aroma. Avoid moisture, which will make the cookies lose their crispness.

fried-summer-squash-yellow-or-green.title: Fried Summer Squash, Yellow or Green

content.title: About
content.content: Fried summer squash (yellow or green) consists of thin slices of squash quickly cooked in vegetable oil until golden and crisp. The squash has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture, while frying enhances its aroma and makes it more satisfying.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Summer squash belongs to the cucurbit family and is harvested in warm months.
Yellow squash contains more carotenoids, giving it its bright hue, compared with green varieties.
Squash is about 95 % water, so even after frying it remains relatively low‑calorie.
Fried squash is a traditional side dish in Mediterranean cuisine.
Squash readily absorbs herbs and spices, making it popular with garlic, paprika, or fresh herbs.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Even when fried, squash stays relatively low‑calorie, making it suitable for weight‑conscious diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Squash provides vitamin B6 and folate, which support metabolism and nervous‑system health.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Yellow squash supplies beta‑carotene, while green squash offers lutein—both protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in squash promotes regular bowel movements and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in fluid balance and blood‑pressure regulation.

items.title: High fat content when fried
items.content: Using a lot of oil can significantly increase the dish’s calorie count.

items.title: Cucurbit allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to squash.

items.title: Risk of acrylamide
items.content: Over‑cooking can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fried squash hot as a side, snack, or topping for salads. Sprinkle with salt, spices, grated cheese, or a squeeze of lemon. It pairs well with yogurt‑based dips, tahini, or tomato sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fried squash in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the oven or skillet to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: The chocolate chip muffin is a soft, mildly sweet baked good made from wheat flour, eggs, milk, butter, and chocolate chip pieces. It offers a fragrant vanilla flavor and a slight crunch from the chocolate chips, making it a popular breakfast item and snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first muffin recipes appeared in the United States in the early 20th century.
Chocolate chips are usually small chunks of chocolate or specially formulated chips that retain their shape during baking.
Muffins are often served warm, with a moist interior and a lightly golden top.
There are many variations: with berries, nuts, citrus zest, or even spices.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates and a modest amount of fat provide a quick energy boost, ideal for a morning meal.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs and milk contribute a modest amount of animal protein that supports tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Dairy ingredients supply calcium for bone health, while vitamin D aids its absorption.

items.title: Antioxidants from chocolate
items.content: Chocolate chips contain flavonoids that may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet muffins can raise blood glucose levels, especially for people with diabetes.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Milk and butter may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of butter and sugar, muffins are relatively calorie‑dense and should be eaten in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chocolate chip muffins can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, sliced and spread with cream cheese, paired with yogurt or fresh berries. They are especially aromatic when warm, but retain flavor when eaten cold.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Reheat in a microwave or oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Nutritional Powder Mix is a high‑protein blend designed to support muscle recovery and increase daily protein intake. It contains fast‑digesting whey protein along with additional nutrients for optimal nutrition.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Each serving provides over 30 g of protein.
Formulated with digestive enzymes for better absorption.
Suitable for athletes and active‑lifestyle individuals.
Gluten‑ and lactose‑free, compatible with most diets.
Neutral flavor mixes easily with water, milk, or juice.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Helps rebuild and grow muscle mass after workouts.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Contains B‑vitamins and zinc that support normal immune function.

items.title: Energy support
items.content: Low‑glycemic carbs provide a steady energy release.

items.title: Improved recovery
items.content: Added BCAA amino acids reduce muscle fatigue.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Includes calcium and vitamin D to strengthen bones.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Contains whey protein, which may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Excessive protein intake
items.content: Very high protein consumption can strain kidneys in predisposed persons.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some versions contain sucralose or aspartame, which may not be suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix one scoop (≈30 g) with 250‑300 ml of water, milk, or plant‑based beverage. It can also be added to smoothies, oatmeal, or baked goods to boost protein content.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place, tightly sealed. For long‑term storage, keep refrigerated to prevent clumping.

content.title: About
content.content: Orange juice 100% no added sugar (NFS) is made from fresh oranges grown in sunny regions. The juice contains no added sugars, preservatives or artificial flavors, preserving the natural taste and aroma of the fruit.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Orange juice is one of the most popular non‑alcoholic beverages worldwide.
Vitamin C in freshly squeezed juice is better preserved than in pasteurized juice when the juice is not subjected to prolonged heating.
Navel oranges are often used for NFS products because of their high sugar content and aroma.
Oranges for juice are usually harvested in the early morning when sugar levels are at their peak.
In some countries orange juice is considered “natural” only if it contains at least 95% pure juice.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially beneficial for pregnant women.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The juice contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: With more than 90% water content, it helps maintain the body’s hydration.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Natural sugars
items.content: Although no sugar is added, the natural sugars can affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to oranges.

items.title: Possible drug interactions
items.content: Large amounts of vitamin C can influence the effectiveness of certain medications, such as anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the juice chilled as a refreshing beverage, use it in smoothies, cocktails, sauces and marinades. To reduce acidity, a small amount of water or honey can be added.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 1 °C to 4 °C. After opening, consume within 3–5 days. Do not keep at room temperature for more than 2 hours to prevent microbial growth.

rice-brown-with-vegetables-and-gravy-no-.title: Brown Rice with Vegetables and Gravy, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain product that retains the bran and germ. In this dish it is served with a mix of vegetables (carrot, broccoli, bell pepper) and a light gravy made from vegetable broth, without any added oil or fat. The meal is rich in fiber, vitamins, and minerals while being low in energy density.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice contains about twice the fiber of white rice.
It retains more B‑vitamins, magnesium, and selenium thanks to the intact bran layer.
Steaming the rice helps preserve the maximum amount of nutrients.
The vegetables can be seasonal, influencing both flavor and antioxidant content.
Fat‑free gravy is usually prepared from vegetable stock, tomato puree, or aromatic herbs.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the whole grain and vegetables promotes intestinal motility and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Helps regulate blood sugar
items.content: The low glycemic index of brown rice aids in preventing post‑meal glucose spikes.

items.title: Rich source of vitamins and minerals
items.content: The dish provides vitamins A, C, K, as well as magnesium, phosphorus, and iron, essential for metabolic processes.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Absence of added fats and presence of plant antioxidants contribute to lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Immune system boost
items.content: Vitamins C and A from the vegetables enhance the body’s defense mechanisms.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to rice.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in excess.

items.title: Food poisoning risk
items.content: Improperly stored rice can harbor Bacillus cereus; cool quickly and refrigerate.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The dish can be served as a standalone meal or as a side to meat, fish, or tofu. It reheats well in the microwave or on the stovetop, and fresh herbs can be added for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it remains good for up to 2 months if portioned beforehand.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg drop soup is a classic Chinese broth in which beaten eggs are slowly poured into hot stock, forming delicate ribbons. The dish is usually made with chicken or vegetable broth, seasoned with soy sauce, ginger, and sometimes a touch of cornstarch for a light thickening.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The soup originated in Hunan province and quickly spread throughout China.
Eggs are added as a thin stream, creating the characteristic "fluffy" appearance.
Traditional recipes use chicken broth, but vegetarian versions use vegetable stock.
It is often served as a light starter or the first course of a multi‑course meal.
Some regions garnish the soup with scallions, sesame oil, or white pepper for extra flavor.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete source of high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Low‑calorie yet nourishing
items.content: The soup is low in calories but supplies important micronutrients such as iron and vitamin B12.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: Chicken broth contains glycine and other amino acids that help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Warm broth is gentle on the stomach and can be soothing during a cold.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The broth provides potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus, which are vital for heart and bone health.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: People with egg allergy may experience reactions ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared soup often includes soy sauce, raising the salt level; those with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Food‑borne risk
items.content: If the broth is not brought to a full boil, harmful bacteria may survive.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; individuals with elevated cholesterol should consume in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot in a deep bowl. Pour beaten eggs in a thin stream into the boiling broth while stirring constantly to create fine ribbons. Optionally garnish with sliced scallions, a drizzle of sesame oil, or a splash of soy sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftover soup in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat to a rolling boil before serving to ensure safety.
